messages.author: 17f8070912132195
messages.subject: Point process and preferential sampling
parts:
Dear INLA group,


I am considering using a point process to deal with preferential sampling, inspired by Chapter 4 in the book ‘Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA.’


The log-Cox point process model deals with the point pattern (the locations). That is, the response variable is 1 for observations (representing the points) and 0 for mesh nodes:

y.pp <- rep(0:1, c(nv, n))


I want to extend the locations to include sampling durations at each point. That means, for observations, y.pp would be positive continuous values. I plan to use a ‘Tweedie’ likelihood and set the offset E as usual. Is this possible? Really appreciate your guidance.


Thanks,

Ruby

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Point process and preferential sampling
parts:
Hi,

The point process likelihood setup is a very specific construction (or
rather, can be one of several equally specific constructions; the book
uses a different method than the implementation in inlabru, which is
based on the "Going off grid" paper.
What you're describing would either be a completely separate model
(there's no direct link between a Poisson point process likelihood and
the Tweedie distribution), or not a point process variation, but
rather a variation of an aggregated _count_ observation model, or a
third thing. Which it is depends on _precisely_ what you mean. Are the
"sampling durations" a measure of local sampling effort? Then you
don't have a Poisson point process. Or are they "an event that lasted
this long was observed at this location"? THen it may be a version of
a point process, possibly a "marked point process".
Before you've figured out precisely the _model_ you want is, it's
impossible to give advice on how to implement it.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Point process and preferential sampling
parts:
I missed the "preferential sampling" part; that usually involves
having a model for observability or sampling effort for _every_ point
in space, _not_ just where you observed points, i.e. it's a sampling
effort model, where the observability may be dependent on the true
intensity field for the point process model.
Is that what you're looking for?

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Point process and preferential sampling
parts:
OK, so the confusion is that you talked about the "sampling duration"
at each observed point, but the sampling effort is not a value
observed for each observation, but instead has to be known or modelled
for _every_ location in space.

A regular point pattern model is
{y_i} ~ PoissonProcess(E \lambda(s))
with constant sampling effort E, or
{y_i} ~ PoissonProcess(E(s) \lambda(s))
with spatially varying sampling effort E(s).

To estimate such models, you have to either known E(s), or be able to
model it using some kind of observations of it.
There have been different approaches to this in the literature, but
the easiest is if you have sampling effort information that isn't tied
to the observed points, but rather known or observed by other means.
Assuming that you're able to write a joint model for E(s) and \lambdas(s), then
\eta_apparent(s) = \log(\lambda(s)) + \log(E(s))
is the \log of the _apparent_ point process intensity, i.e. of the
observed point pattern when the true point pattern would have
intensity \lambda(s),
and your observed point pattern is a conditional Poisson point process
{y_i}|\eta_apparent ~ PoissonProcess(\exp(\eta_apparent(s)))

Such models can in principle be implemented with inlabru (see the LGCP
examples at https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/articles.html),
as they are a variation of distance sampling models, where the
sampling effort is modelled as a function of distance to the observer,
independent of the true lambda.
In the preferential sampling setting, it's more likely that E has some
features in common with \lambda. The models are fundamentally
non-identifiable unless one can constrain the effort model somewhow.

What you mentioned about using a Tweedie observation model seems to be
a completely different approach that I can't help you with.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Point process and preferential sampling
parts:
In the point process itself, the observations are the locations of the points, and the sampling domain. 0/1 variables only come in when constructing the likelihood information for inla(), and whether that uses 0/1 variables or other values depend on the specific implementation. For example, in inlabru, the default Cox process likelihood construction has a single likelihood contribution for all of the observed points, with “y” for that contribution being equal to the total number of observed points, and zero for each spatial integration point contribution. Other equivalent approaches are possible.
Finn
